NHI 2018 - WHAT's WHAT?

By: Nicky Troll | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
While the details of the implementation of the National Health Insurance Plan are sketchy, a few things are certain – it’s coming, it will be mandatory and you, the taxpayer, will be paying for it

Unique Selling Point:
• Topical
• Time for South Africans to make their voices known.
• It affects everyone!

Summary:
I propose a shorter 8-minute piece looking at four aspects:

- What does it mean for Doctors?
- What does it mean for Medical Aids and Private Health Care?
- How do we compare internationally in terms of GDP and affordability?
- Is this a solution for us – is it the silver bullet our health system so desperately needs?

I propose interviewing three experts, using links and info graphic types images to help tell the story simply and concisely without getting caught up in the unknowns and speculation.

INTERVIEWEES
– SA Medical Association (Sama) - spokesperson Dr Mzukisi Grootboom.
– Alex van den Heever – WITS, Chair, Social Security Systems Administration and Management studies - researching health reform for over 20 years
– ECONEX – HEALTHCARE CONSULTANCY OF ACTURARIES & ECONOMISTS


Further information:
NOT THE SILVER BULLET
- This system is designed for corruption with too much power seated in a single person’s hands….
- We are mimicing the UK’s NHS that is not designed for South Africa’s problems….
- Systematic problems in the Department has to be addressed.

While the public health system is desperately under-funded, money alone will not fix it. Yet this is the underlying assumption of the National Health Insurance (NHI) Bill, which serves to force the public and private health systems into a hasty marriage.
South Africa has poor health outcomes compared to other middle-income countries such as Brazil with similar health spending as a percentage of GDP. It spends more than R300 billion – or around 8.5% of its gross domestic product – on health care. But half is spent in the private sector catering for people who are well off while the remaining 84% of the population, which carries a far greater burden of disease, depends on the under-resourced public sector.
Poor management of every aspect of public health - finances, human resources, procurement and maintenance - is one of the biggest weaknesses of the sector. More money in the system will not remedy this. It will simply provide incompetent and corrupt managers with bigger budgets to burn. The health system performs poorly due to a combination of factors including the poor management of public sector hospitals, health professional shortages (particularly in rural areas), low productivity levels among staff, escalating private health care costs and poor quality of care.
But in its current form the proposed legislation won’t be a silver bullet. There are still too many inconsistencies and unanswered questions for it to be the final roadmap to universal health care in the country.
THE BASICS
IDEALISTIC GOALS
• The bill is informed by a vision of ensuring equitable access to quality health services, regardless of a person’s ability to pay or whether they live in an urban or rural area.
• Aimed at all South Africans‚ the NHI will dictate that there will be no fees charged at health facility because the NHI fund will cover the costs of care.
• The proposed insurance fund envisages the consolidation of public and private revenue into one funding pool.
• NHI will be run as a non-profit public entity aimed at strengthening the hand of the healthcare consumer and keeping the cost of healthcare reasonable while ensuring that healthcare providers receive fair rate for their services.
• Through the fund, registered members have the right to quality healthcare, free of charge, from certified and accredited providers. These providers, in turn, will be fully reimbursed by the fund.
• The only time that treatment won’t be funded is when there is no medical necessity for the treatment or there is no cost-effective intervention for the service. In such cases, members need to be informed and can also challenge the decision.
THE REALITY
• The NHI would make all South Africans dependent on a single state-run medical scheme: the NHI fund.
• The Davis tax committee warned in 2017 that an NHI would not be sustainable without much faster growth, which is unlikely to happen.
• Motsoaledi has made it clear under NHI, the rich will subsidise the poor. The young will subsidise the old. The healthy will subsidise the sick. The urban will subsidise the rural.
• The money for the NHI Bill will not be coming from the Health Ministry's budget but from the national public purse.
• MOTSOALEDI: “NHI is going to be a mandatory for health services, meaning once it’s a law, all South Africans will need to contribute into it if Treasury rules that it is to be funded through contributions from the population. // We don’t know what they’re going to rule but if it’s mandatory, it means you can’t opt out of it, just like the Constitution.”
• “While the bill is still being debated, we’re not going to wait. We’re going to implement four NHI projects. Remember that Treasury gave us R4.1 billion to provide services.”

How it will work
• According to the bill, the fund has to cover comprehensive health service
• All people will have to register as users of the fund at an accredited health care establishment or facility (whether public or private).
• The fund will decide on the health benefits that the facilities will have to provide. This will depend on what resources the facility has.
• No other healthcare services (specialists or hospitals) can be sought out unless referred by that primary provider under the NHI.
THE STRUCTURE THAT’S BEEN PROPOSED FOR THE FUND IS RAISING CONCERNS ON TWO FRONTS: IT APPEARS UNNECESSARILY CUMBERSOME AND THERE’S A LACK OF CLARITY ON LINES OF COMMAND.
DOCTORS AND THE NHI
There is very little clarity on how it will affect Doctors – they will essentially have to become available to service both private and public healthcare. To be paid, health care providers, such as general practitioners and hospitals, will have to register with the fund. They will have to claim for each patient that they treat and will have to keep a record of diagnosis, treatment and length of stay.
The questions are
• how will it be run
• how much will they be paid
• and how many patients will they be required to see?

It could mean that we will see a number of qualified GPs leaving the country.

SAMA a non-statutory, professional association for public and private sector medical practitioners has openly critised the NHI bill.

PRIVATE HEALTH CARE & MEDICAL AIDS
Despite government's intention to introduce a single health system with compulsory contributions from all working South Africans, it may be impossible to outlaw private healthcare.

"The National Health Insurance (NHI) Bill is obscure about whether people can buy cover outside of the national scheme, and refers to private cover that is complementary," said Van den Heever.

Many South Africans though fear that the NHI will aim to scrap private health care – but it appears that it would not be such an easy feat for government.

"But you cannot just remove a right. The NHI is insurance, not a service. Canada tried to prohibit people from having private healthcare and they lost a court challenge. Prohibition serves no public purpose or social benefit."

• the greatest likelihood is that medical aids will become a supplementary system to the NHI, but questions remain how this will work.
“Medical schemes may end up performing a supplementary role in the provision of healthcare services to South Africans – primarily, as a top-up device or ancillary provider of services not offered by NHI,” he said.
• Schemes may decide to cut down what they cover – or there may be convergence among different groups.

The Medical Schemes Amendment Bill contains measures to improve scheme governance, expand mandatory benefits to include more primary healthcare cover and regulate broker fees more closely.
While it does not detail the fees healthcare providers may charge medical scheme members, Motsoaledi reiterated his stance that there should be a uniform tariff.

THE ECONOMICS OF IT ALL

• The introduction of National Health Insurance (NHI) was likely to cost South Africa more than R600 billion at its start in 2026, with costs continuing to escalate thereafter, according to the South African Institute of Race Relations (SAIRR).
• SAIRR head of policy research Anthea Jeffrey cautioned government on the “dire implications” of introducing a medical health scheme South Africa could not afford.
“No proper costing has ever been done on the NHI. The projected R256 billion in the 2025 figure provided in the 2017 white paper is a 2010 figure, which is badly outdated and entirely unrealistic.
• “At present, 85% of public hospitals and clinics could not be accredited to take part in the NHI because they are unable to comply adequately with basic healthcare norms and standards, such as maintaining proper hygiene and having medicines available.
• the NHI would lead to existing medical schemes being “squeezed out of existence, leaving the middle-class dependent solely on the NHI.”

Healthcare consultancy Econex did a lot of financial / budget research around the Davis Commission.

PILOT PROGRAMMES – WE’VE BEEN DOWN THIS ROAD
Treasury initially allocated R 1 Billion for the pilot programme – but then slashed funding because of slow spending by the provinces. Latest figures from the Dept of Health show the NHI pilot districts have collectively spent R145 million of the R200.4 million allocated via the NHI grant in the four years to March 2016.
NHI pilot studies do not address the differences in the funding model that would pertain under NHI. Pilot sites are thus not a reflection of the actual way NHI will be run at all, as the largest component in NHI is the single funder payment model. Doing the cost projections for this funding model is thus of the utmost importance, to determine affordability.
The office of Health Standards Compliance inspection records show that NHI pilot sites are failing to improve any faster than those in the rest of the country. Of the 1427 facilities inspected in the four years to March 2016 – just 89 of them scored a pass mark of 70% or more. The department of health disputes these stats.

Government has tried to contract private doctors to work in public health facilities in its NHI pilot districts, but it has only managed to attract 342 doctors. Only a third of GPs who were contracted said they would stay, blaming lack of equipment and poor working conditions, according to research published in the SA Medical Journal in November 2016.


THERE ARE NO OFFICIAL REPORTS ON THE OUTCOMES OF THE PILOT SITES. AND NOW WE ARE THROWING ANOTHER R4 BILLION AT ANOTHER ROLL OUT PROJECT….

Press Release:


South Africa’s public healthcare is desperately under-funded with serious staff shortages, collapsing infrastructure and it’s overburdened with patients. Government believes that the proposed National Health Insurance Plan will be the panacea to saving a system in crisis. While the details of the implementation of the NHI may be sketchy, a few things are certain – it is coming, it will be mandatory and the taxpayer will be paying for it. Carte Blanche analyses whether this plan really is the silver bullet.

Script:


STRUCTURE: NHI

VO: Last week we exposed the chronic failures in the Health Department from severe staff shortages to crumbling infrastructure and overcrowded hospitals across three provinces.

Crisis after Crisis, - provincial health departments are plagued by failures in finance, human resources, procurement and general management.

UPSOUND: I would rather die

From LIFE Esidemeni, to ongoing KZN’s Oncology crisis, to the Free State's shocking maternal mortality rates – all under the Health Minister Aaron Motsoaledi’s watch.

LINK: It’s no secret that state health is in a critical condition across the country...the system is strained and equipment is falling apart – corruption and mismanagement are a daily prescription.

VO: But the National Health Insurance and Medical Schemes Amendment Bills are being hailed as the cure-all.

MINISTER UPSOUND PRESS CONFERENCE: [21 JUNE 2018]
"We need a massive re-organisation of the whole healthcare system in both public and private.” [42.36]

VO: As it stands, roughly 16% (8 945 600) of the population belong to private medical aid schemes - it accounts for more than half [51.76%] of South Africa's entire health spend.

The remaining 84% (46 964 400) of the population relies on the overburdened public healthcare system with less than half [48.24%] of the country's health spend.

So what’s the goal of the NHI? To pool all healthcare funds and provide free health services to all citizens.

MINISTER UPSOUND PRESS CONFERENCE: [21 JUNE 2018]
“The rich will subsidise the poor, the young will subsidise the old, and the healthy must subsidise the sick." [29.15]

VO: BUT IS THE NHI THE MAGIC BULLET? [DEVICE]

SASHA: the devil in health system reform is in the detail and we don’t have that detail. INT1 M16
LINK: The details of the implementation of the National Health Insurance Plan are sketchy, a few things are certain – it’s coming, it will be mandatory and you, the taxpayer, will foot the bill [OPENING LINK]

VO: While a more equitable system with shared health resources is a concept supported by public interest law centre, Section27 – lawyer Sasha Stevenson is concerned that it skirts around the big issues.

SASHA: The bill doesn’t deal with reform of the public health system, improving it to the extent that would be required to provide universal health coverage, it doesn’t deal with regulation of the private health care system that would be required, it doesn’t put in place governance and leadership mechanism that are required // INT1 M15

VO: Health Reform Expert Alex van den Heever believes there are gaping holes in the current NHI Bill.

ALEX: it provides no guarantees that anything we are seeing today will change – // // these gaps will grow, cover in public and private healthcare will get more expensive // we will pay more and get less value. INT1 M31

VO: While sections of the Bill are reasonable, many aspects are vague according Dr. Mzukisi Grootboom. He is from the South African Medical Association, representing doctors in the public and private sector.

GROOTBOOM: what the government is proposing is only one aspect of a health service – it’s one pillar of the health system and it’s the funding mechanism of how you fund that activity INT2 M14

VO: But will it pave the way for improved medical treatment for all?

Some feel even the timing of the health reform bills is suspicious with the 2019 elections creeping up.

GROOTBOOM: //I want to warn south Africans – they have got something coming – they need to hold ANC government to task about the promises they made about health care – and NHI is not the magic bullet. INT2 M16

VO: Health Minister, Aaron Motsoaledi, disagrees.

MINISTER: if it is just a PR exercise it wont resolve the problems of the country and by they way is in the National development plan INT2 M6 // it’s not something we thumbsucked – it is a system that has been studied by experts // INT2M7

LINK: It’s a wonderful concept.... no fees to pay and expert care at improved health facilities....the NHI fund will pick up the tab and pay all the medical specialists. But, in reality, does the maths in the NHI bill add up.

VO: By the minister’s own admission, the initial R256 Billion budget was more guesswork than fact . Health economists put the figures closer to the R600-billion-mark .

BUT CAN WE AFFORD IT? [DEVICE]

It would require a massive tax rise, which would neccissitate taxpayers like you - to cough up even more. Van den Heever believes it’s just not realistic in our current economic climate.

ALEX: if you look at those objective and what they should cost if we were to achieve them – we can not afford it.

VO: The fund is set to cover a range of medical services, treatments and procedures – the bill just doesn’t specify what these will be….

MINISTER: The reason is that if you put them there and it becomes an Act you have to ammend an Act all the time.

VO: The idea is that basic services would be covered by the NHI and elective treatments would not.

So, WHAT’S THE FUTURE OF MEDICAL AIDS? [DEVICE]

Well - it is clear in the bill’s current form, that private medical aid cover will be limited explains Van den Heever.

ALEX: Part of they way in which they would attempt to ensure that you only have a single gate keeper to contracting or reimbursement – is to prevent medical schemes from reimbursing any benefit that is covered by the health insurance fund which means you wouldn’t be able to buy private insurance cover for anything that is covered by this fund

VO: But Van den Heever says it’s highly unlikely that private medical aids will be scrapped completely - it was attempted in Canada and it failed.

ALEX: – we cannot convert the coverage which we have in the medical scheme system into a state version and do that without // harming health care in South Africa.

VO: And, HOW WILL IT IMPACT ON MEDICAL PRACTITIONERS? [DEVICE]

They would need to be accredited with the NHI and will then be paid by the fund – not by you, the patient. Sounds simple - but will this work? Doctors are doubtful says Dr. Grootboom.

GROOTBOOM: there is a lot uncertainty, there is a lot anxiety and part of that is because there is no clear cut mechanism of how that system is going to be implemented – people are concerned about their futures, their earning capacity, //INT1 M4

VO: The quality of healthcare is also a huge concern for SAMA.

GROOTBOOM: What is not coming out in the current bill is the fact that when the dept says it wants to make healthcare facilities of a good quality – they do not define the quality that they are talking about. INT1 M14

LINK: Almost 6 years ago government appointed a number pilot sights at an initial cost of R1 billion – the goal of project was quite simply to test run the NHI…the results are yet to materialise.

SASHA: there were no proper business plans which was an issue that we raised right at the beginning - so it was never clear what the plan was INT1 M17

MINISTER: INT1 M8 I realise that the word pilot was not clearly understand – the NHI is a fund – we are not testing a fund, we are testing several things which we want to happen….

VO: The minister explained that the project tested various possible interventions which will become necessary in the NHI – these included community healthcare, school health and contracting GPs.

Although the Minister says these projects were a success – Stevenson is less convinced - without official public reports, she believes the pilot projects missed the mark.

SASHA: it’s (?) an opportunity to test what worked, to see different funding mechanisms would work but we haven’t seen what’s happened out of the NHI pilot districts // so we’ve lost the opportunity to gain insights from the piloting sites INT1 M17

VO: The NHI proposal puts too much power in the hands of the health minister according to Van den Heever – he says it’s designed for corruption.

ALEX: It essentially centralises decision making using a patronage model of governance. INT1 M38 // it creates a gatekeeper model where a single person controls too many points of decision making in a structure – you will not find that in the NHS in the UK or anywhere in Europe. INT1

VO: Minister Motsoaledi doesn’t seem to think it’s a problem.

MINSITER: INT2 M1 I don’t think there is anything wrong with a political appointment – if you appoint the right people – the problem is if it political appointment and there is patronage, cronyism//

VO: These problems are deeply rooted and need to be adequately addressed.

SASHA: We’re in a very difficult place and we need to be moving to a much more quickly towards a more equitable health system. INT1 M19//The NHI provides an end goal, it doesn’t provide a path//INT1 M14

VO: While we don’t know what the NHI will cover, how much it will cost and what it will mean for healthcare professionals – we do know a lot needs to be changed before South Africa can achieve acceptable standards of universal healthcare.

GROOTBOOM: INT2 M15 we are seeing a situation where there is a dichotomy between good policies and poor outcomes. We cannot allow that to continue – we must not be hoodwinked by people who are saying //Don’t worry the NHI is around the corner – it will cure all this – it’s not the case.





PROMOS

PROMO 1
VO: Is the proposed the NHI the cure all for South Africa’s overburdened public health system?

SASHA: the devil in health system reform is in the detail and we don’t have that detail. INT1

PROMO 2
VO: National Health Insurance is coming – it will be mandatory and you the taxpayer will foot the bill – but can the country really afford it?

ALEX: if you look at those objective and what they should cost if we were to achieve them – we can not afford it. INT1 M33

PROMO 3
VO: Is the NHI the magic bullet for our crippled public health system – experts are doubtful.

GROOTBOOM: INT2 M15 we are seeing a situation where there is a dichotomy between good policies and poor outcomes. We cannot allow that to continue

PROMO 4

VO: National Health Insurance is coming – it will be mandatory and you the taxpayer will foot the bill.

UPSOUND MOTSOALEDI:
“The rich must subsidise the poor, the young must subsidise the old, and the healthy must subsidise the sick."

SASHA: the devil in health system reform is in the detail and we don’t have that detail. INT1

PILOT PROGRAMMES – WE’VE BEEN DOWN THIS ROAD Treasury initially allocated R 1 Billion for the pilot programme – but then slashed funding because of slow spending by the provinces. Latest figures from the Dept of Health show the NHI pilot districts have collectively spent R145 million of the R200.4 million allocated via the NHI grant in the four years to March 2016. NHI pilot studies do not address the differences in the funding model that would pertain under NHI. Pilot sites are thus not a reflection of the actual way NHI will be run at all, as the largest component in NHI is the single funder payment model. Doing the cost projections for this funding model is thus of the utmost importance, to determine affordability. The office of Health Standards Compliance inspection records show that NHI pilot sites are failing to improve any faster than those in the rest of the country. Of the 1427 facilities inspected in the four years to March 2016 – just 89 of them scored a pass mark of 70% or more. The department of health disputes these stats. Government has tried to contract private doctors to work in public health facilities in its NHI pilot districts, but it has only managed to attract 342 doctors. Only a third of GPs who were contracted said they would stay, blaming lack of equipment and poor working conditions, according to research published in the SA Medical Journal in November 2016. THERE ARE NO OFFICIAL REPORTS ON THE OUTCOMES OF THE PILOT SITES. AND NOW WE ARE THROWING ANOTHER R4 BILLION AT ANOTHER ROLL OUT PROJECT…. While the details of the implementation of the NHI may be sketchy, a few things are certain – it is coming, it will be mandatory and the taxpayer will be paying for it. LINK: It’s no secret that state health is in a critical condition across the country...the system is strained and equipment is falling apart – corruption and mismanagement are a daily prescription. VO: But the National Health Insurance and Medical Schemes Amendment Bills are being hailed as the cure-all. MINISTER UPSOUND PRESS CONFERENCE: [21 JUNE 2018] "We need a massive re-organisation of the whole healthcare system in both public and private.” [42.36] VO: As it stands, roughly 16% (8 945 600) of the population belong to private medical aid schemes - it accounts for more than half [51.76%] of South Africa's entire health spend. The remaining 84% (46 964 400) of the population relies on the overburdened public healthcare system with less than half [48.24%] of the country's health spend. So what’s the goal of the NHI? To pool all healthcare funds and provide free health services to all citizens. MINISTER UPSOUND PRESS CONFERENCE: [21 JUNE 2018] “The rich will subsidise the poor, the young will subsidise the old, and the healthy must subsidise the sick." [29.15] VO: BUT IS THE NHI THE MAGIC BULLET? [DEVICE] SASHA: the devil in health system reform is in the detail and we don’t have that detail. SASHA: The bill doesn’t deal with reform of the public health system, improving it to the extent that would be required to provide universal health coverage, it doesn’t deal with regulation of the private health care system that would be required, it doesn’t put in place governance and leadership mechanism that are required // INT1 M15 VO: Health Reform Expert Alex van den Heever believes there are gaping holes in the current NHI Bill. ALEX: it provides no guarantees that anything we are seeing today will change – // // these gaps will grow, cover in public and private healthcare will get more expensive // we will pay more and get less value. INT1 M31 VO: While sections of the Bill are reasonable, many aspects are vague according Dr. Mzukisi Grootboom. He is from the South African Medical Association, representing doctors in the public and private sector. GROOTBOOM: what the government is proposing is only one aspect of a health service – it’s one pillar of the health system and it’s the funding mechanism of how you fund that activity INT2 M14 VO: But will it pave the way for improved medical treatment for all? Some feel even the timing of the health reform bills is suspicious with the 2019 elections creeping up. GROOTBOOM: //I want to warn south Africans – they have got something coming – they need to hold ANC government to task about the promises they made about health care – and NHI is not the magic bullet. INT2 M16 VO: Health Minister, Aaron Motsoaledi, disagrees. MINISTER: if it is just a PR exercise it wont resolve the problems of the country and by they way is in the National development plan INT2 M6 // it’s not something we thumbsucked – it is a system that has been studied by experts // INT2M7 LINK: It’s a wonderful concept.... no fees to pay and expert care at improved health facilities....the NHI fund will pick up the tab and pay all the medical specialists. ALEX: if you look at those objective and what they should cost if we were to achieve them – we can not afford it. MINISTER: The reason is that if you put them there and it becomes an Act you have to ammend an Act all the time. VO: The idea is that basic services would be covered by the NHI and elective treatments would not. So, WHAT’S THE FUTURE OF MEDICAL AIDS? [DEVICE] Well - it is clear in the bill’s current form, that private medical aid cover will be limited explains Van den Heever. ALEX: Part of they way in which they would attempt to ensure that you only have a single gate keeper to contracting or reimbursement – is to prevent medical schemes from reimbursing any benefit that is covered by the health insurance fund which means you wouldn’t be able to buy private insurance cover for anything that is covered by this fund VO: But Van den Heever says it’s highly unlikely that private medical aids will be scrapped completely - it was attempted in Canada and it failed. ALEX: – we cannot convert the coverage which we have in the medical scheme system into a state version and do that without // harming health care in South Africa. metadata.Summary: I propose a shorter 8-minute piece looking at four aspects: - What does it mean for Doctors? - What does it mean for Medical Aids and Private Health Care? - How do we compare internationally in terms of GDP and affordability? - Is this a solution for us – is it the silver bullet our health system so desperately needs? I propose interviewing three experts, using links and info graphic types images to help tell the story simply and concisely without getting caught up in the unknowns and speculation. INTERVIEWEES – SA Medical Association (Sama) - spokesperson Dr Mzukisi Grootboom. – Alex van den Heever – WITS, Chair, Social Security Systems Administration and Management studies - researching health reform for over 20 years – ECONEX – HEALTHCARE CONSULTANCY OF ACTURARIES & ECONOMISTS
metadata.Further information: NOT THE SILVER BULLET - This system is designed for corruption with too much power seated in a single person’s hands…. - We are mimicing the UK’s NHS that is not designed for South Africa’s problems…. - Systematic problems in the Department has to be addressed. While the public health system is desperately under-funded, money alone will not fix it. Yet this is the underlying assumption of the National Health Insurance (NHI) Bill, which serves to force the public and private health systems into a hasty marriage. South Africa has poor health outcomes compared to other middle-income countries such as Brazil with similar health spending as a percentage of GDP. It spends more than R300 billion – or around 8.5% of its gross domestic product – on health care. But half is spent in the private sector catering for people who are well off while the remaining 84% of the population, which carries a far greater burden of disease, depends on the under-resourced public sector. Poor management of every aspect of public health - finances, human resources, procurement and maintenance - is one of the biggest weaknesses of the sector. More money in the system will not remedy this. It will simply provide incompetent and corrupt managers with bigger budgets to burn. The health system performs poorly due to a combination of factors including the poor management of public sector hospitals, health professional shortages (particularly in rural areas), low productivity levels among staff, escalating private health care costs and poor quality of care. But in its current form the proposed legislation won’t be a silver bullet. There are still too many inconsistencies and unanswered questions for it to be the final roadmap to universal health care in the country. THE BASICS IDEALISTIC GOALS • The bill is informed by a vision of ensuring equitable access to quality health services, regardless of a person’s ability to pay or whether they live in an urban or rural area. • Aimed at all South Africans‚ the NHI will dictate that there will be no fees charged at health facility because the NHI fund will cover the costs of care. • The proposed insurance fund envisages the consolidation of public and private revenue into one funding pool. • NHI will be run as a non-profit public entity aimed at strengthening the hand of the healthcare consumer and keeping the cost of healthcare reasonable while ensuring that healthcare providers receive fair rate for their services. • Through the fund, registered members have the right to quality healthcare, free of charge, from certified and accredited providers. These providers, in turn, will be fully reimbursed by the fund. • The only time that treatment won’t be funded is when there is no medical necessity for the treatment or there is no cost-effective intervention for the service. In such cases, members need to be informed and can also challenge the decision. THE REALITY • The NHI would make all South Africans dependent on a single state-run medical scheme: the NHI fund. • The Davis tax committee warned in 2017 that an NHI would not be sustainable without much faster growth, which is unlikely to happen. • Motsoaledi has made it clear under NHI, the rich will subsidise the poor. The young will subsidise the old. The healthy will subsidise the sick. The urban will subsidise the rural. • The money for the NHI Bill will not be coming from the Health Ministry's budget but from the national public purse. • MOTSOALEDI: “NHI is going to be a mandatory for health services, meaning once it’s a law, all South Africans will need to contribute into it if Treasury rules that it is to be funded through contributions from the population. // We don’t know what they’re going to rule but if it’s mandatory, it means you can’t opt out of it, just like the Constitution.” • “While the bill is still being debated, we’re not going to wait. We’re going to implement four NHI projects. Remember that Treasury gave us R4.1 billion to provide services.” How it will work • According to the bill, the fund has to cover comprehensive health service • All people will have to register as users of the fund at an accredited health care establishment or facility (whether public or private). • The fund will decide on the health benefits that the facilities will have to provide. This will depend on what resources the facility has. • No other healthcare services (specialists or hospitals) can be sought out unless referred by that primary provider under the NHI. THE STRUCTURE THAT’S BEEN PROPOSED FOR THE FUND IS RAISING CONCERNS ON TWO FRONTS: IT APPEARS UNNECESSARILY CUMBERSOME AND THERE’S A LACK OF CLARITY ON LINES OF COMMAND. DOCTORS AND THE NHI There is very little clarity on how it will affect Doctors – they will essentially have to become available to service both private and public healthcare. To be paid, health care providers, such as general practitioners and hospitals, will have to register with the fund. They will have to claim for each patient that they treat and will have to keep a record of diagnosis, treatment and length of stay. The questions are • how will it be run • how much will they be paid • and how many patients will they be required to see? It could mean that we will see a number of qualified GPs leaving the country. SAMA a non-statutory, professional association for public and private sector medical practitioners has openly critised the NHI bill. PRIVATE HEALTH CARE & MEDICAL AIDS Despite government's intention to introduce a single health system with compulsory contributions from all working South Africans, it may be impossible to outlaw private healthcare. "The National Health Insurance (NHI) Bill is obscure about whether people can buy cover outside of the national scheme, and refers to private cover that is complementary," said Van den Heever. Many South Africans though fear that the NHI will aim to scrap private health care – but it appears that it would not be such an easy feat for government. "But you cannot just remove a right. The NHI is insurance, not a service. Canada tried to prohibit people from having private healthcare and they lost a court challenge. Prohibition serves no public purpose or social benefit." • the greatest likelihood is that medical aids will become a supplementary system to the NHI, but questions remain how this will work. “Medical schemes may end up performing a supplementary role in the provision of healthcare services to South Africans – primarily, as a top-up device or ancillary provider of services not offered by NHI,” he said. • Schemes may decide to cut down what they cover – or there may be convergence among different groups. The Medical Schemes Amendment Bill contains measures to improve scheme governance, expand mandatory benefits to include more primary healthcare cover and regulate broker fees more closely. While it does not detail the fees healthcare providers may charge medical scheme members, Motsoaledi reiterated his stance that there should be a uniform tariff. THE ECONOMICS OF IT ALL • The introduction of National Health Insurance (NHI) was likely to cost South Africa more than R600 billion at its start in 2026, with costs continuing to escalate thereafter, according to the South African Institute of Race Relations (SAIRR). • SAIRR head of policy research Anthea Jeffrey cautioned government on the “dire implications” of introducing a medical health scheme South Africa could not afford. “No proper costing has ever been done on the NHI. The projected R256 billion in the 2025 figure provided in the 2017 white paper is a 2010 figure, which is badly outdated and entirely unrealistic. • “At present, 85% of public hospitals and clinics could not be accredited to take part in the NHI because they are unable to comply adequately with basic healthcare norms and standards, such as maintaining proper hygiene and having medicines available. • the NHI would lead to existing medical schemes being “squeezed out of existence, leaving the middle-class dependent solely on the NHI.” Healthcare consultancy Econex did a lot of financial / budget research around the Davis Commission.
